title: Getting back to exercise after an injury: safe steps
intro: After an injury, the safest way is to start lower than before and build up slowly. If the injury is still fresh or you recently had surgery, see a doctor or physio first before starting.
muscles: This routine lightly targets the whole body: legs, glutes, core and shoulders. The focus is on rebuilding strength and confidence in moving, with no jumping and no deep squats.
steps: Start with 5 minutes of slow walking to warm up.
Sit-to-stand from a chair: sit down slowly, stand back up using your legs, hands can help.
Wall push: stand facing a wall, push your body towards the wall and back.
Heel raises while holding a chair, then lower slowly.
Stand on one leg for 10-20 seconds with your hand near a chair for balance.
Finish with slow walking and light stretching.
mistakes: Going straight back to the same heavy workouts as before the injury.
Ignoring pain and carrying on because it feels 'not enough'.
Training hard one day, then resting for a week. Consistency matters more.
easier: Reduce reps to 5, or do everything seated: leg straightening from a chair, arm raises, and ankle pumps.
harder: Add reps or one more round each week, not everything at once. Then try sit-to-stand without using your hands, and push-ups against a lower table. Still avoid jumping until your doctor or physio allows it.
dose: 8-10 reps per movement, 1-2 rounds, 2-3 times a week. Sessions of 10-20 minutes. Only increase slowly if your body feels okay the next day.
safety: Stop if there is sharp pain, increasing swelling, dizziness or chest pain. After surgery or a new injury, get clearance from your doctor or physio first and follow their programme.

faq.q: How do I know if the pain is normal or dangerous?
faq.a: Mild muscle soreness that goes away in 1-2 days is usually okay. Sharp pain, pain at the injured joint, swelling or numbness are signs to stop and see a doctor or physio.

faq.q: I gained weight while resting because of my injury. What now?
faq.a: That's common, don't blame yourself. Start with your eating first, for example watch your rice portion and add vegetables and protein. Movement can be added slowly when your body is ready.

faq.q: When can I go back to jumping or running?
faq.a: It depends on your type of injury and your recovery. Ask your doctor or physio. Usually you need to be able to walk briskly, climb stairs and stand steadily on one leg without pain first.
